title: The Map Room: Answering Geographic Questions by Hand
text:
Ask a geographic information system (GIS) how many acres of a national forest were damaged by insects this year, owner by owner, and it answers in seconds. It lays a map of the damage over a map of who owns the land, keeps the places where the two overlap, and adds up their area.
Before computers, people answered questions like that by hand, in map rooms. They lined up the paper maps, traced one onto film, and laid it over the other on a glass table lit from below. Then they measured every patch where the two overlapped, with a wheeled instrument called a planimeter or by counting dots on a transparent grid. The work was careful and slow, and a new question, such as the same damage by watershed instead of by owner, meant starting most of it over. In a map room, there was no such thing as a quick answer or a quick map.
The map room is where this series, The Shape-Files, begins, because the first geographic information systems were built to take over that work.
The US Forest Service’s Pacific Northwest Region answered that question by hand long after those systems arrived. In 1979, as they had every year since 1947, its crews flew over the forests of Oregon and Washington.1 They drew the damage from insects and disease onto paper maps, one outlined patch at a time. Back in the office, staff measured each patch by hand, with a planimeter or a dot grid, and added up the acres inside every reporting area and every landowner’s property (Fig. 1).2,3
It was a job with two sets of boundaries, the damage and the property lines, and the answer lay where they overlapped. Done by hand, work like that came in four jobs: make the sheets agree, lay one over the other, measure each patch, and add up the patches.

title: The Map Room: Answering Geographic Questions by Hand
section: First, make the sheets agree
text:
First, make the sheets agree
Two maps can be compared only if they share a scale, the ratio between a distance on the map and the same distance on the ground, and the same sheet edges. In Canada, the standard topographic sheets are drawn at 1:50,000, where 1 cm on the map stands for 500 m on the ground,4 and it takes 13,150 of them to cover the country.5 Maps from different offices didn’t always match, so the first job was often redrawing one to fit the other.
Even matching sheets didn’t stay matched, because paper swells in damp air and shrinks in dry air. As early as 1928, the US Geological Survey (USGS) told its field surveyors to fix their sheets to the plane table, a drawing board on a tripod, “by brass thumbscrews or tacks, to reduce to a minimum the expansion or contraction caused by changes in climatic conditions.”6 Printers fought the same problem. Erwin Raisz, a cartographer at Harvard, explained in his textbook that each color of a map was drawn on its own sheet, “usually made on vellum because it does not change its shape and size with humidity.” Each drawing, he added, “must have register marks for perfect overprint,” so that every color printed in exactly the right place.7
Lining sheets up this way is called registration. Laying many sheets side by side raised a second issue. The same USGS instructions noted that neighboring sheets would in theory leave “small gores,” thin gaps, between rows laid edge to edge.6 Each sheet uses a map projection, a way of drawing part of the curved Earth on a flat surface, so in theory a block of sheets can’t be fitted together perfectly. The instructions said the paper’s stretch was the bigger of the two errors. The curve itself is the subject of File 002, How Humans Learned to Measure the Earth.

title: The Map Room: Answering Geographic Questions by Hand
section: Then, lay one over the other
text:
Then, lay one over the other
Seeing one sheet through another took a table lit from below. When the draftsman Eric Tallis joined the drawing office of Britain’s Geological Survey in 1946, the office’s light box “contained about 30 tungsten lamps and in use became hot enough to fry an egg.”8 The office’s history doesn’t say whether anyone brought breakfast. Raisz’s 1948 textbook describes a smaller light table, an 8-by-10-inch pane of thick glass set into a drawing table with a lamp underneath, “a simpler arrangement than the large tracing table with a glass top and a number of lamps.” “Copying maps and drawing color overlays,” a caption in his book says, “is best done over the transparent table.”7
For the damage tally, both sets of lines had to end up on one sheet. On the map in Fig. 1, the ownership boundaries and their hand-written key sit in orange on the same sheet as the damage outlines. Any patch of damage that crossed a property line had to be split along it, so each owner’s share could be measured. The Forest Service was still tracing paper maps over a light table in the 1990s, to prepare them for digitizing (Fig. 2).


Fig. 2In about 1994, a Forest Service technician in Portland, Oregon, traces a paper map onto film over a light table to prepare it for digitizing. The lamp underneath makes the map’s lines show through the film.Photo: Julie Johnson, USDA Forest Service, Region 6 · Public domain · Flickr

Each tracing was another copy of the lines, and another chance for them to slip out of register.

title: The Map Room: Answering Geographic Questions by Hand
section: Then, measure every patch
text:
Then, measure every patch
Turning an outline, however careful, into a number took an instrument that dated from the 1850s. The Swiss mathematician Jakob Amsler designed the polar planimeter in 1854 and described it in print in 1856.9,10 It has two arms, hinged together (Fig. 3). One ends in the pole, a weighted point pressed into the paper. The other carries a small measuring wheel and ends in a tracing point. The technician set the tracing point on the outline, read the wheel, traced the outline clockwise back to the start, and read the wheel again. The difference between the two readings gave the area on the map, and a constant for the map’s scale turned it into acres or hectares.11


Fig. 3A polar planimeter made in Germany for the American instrument maker Keuffel & Esser. The weighted pole arm (top) pivots on the tracing arm (middle), which carries the measuring wheel and dials; the bar below checks the reading against a known area.Photo: Central Intelligence Agency · U.S. government work · Flickr · cropped

The wheel does the measuring. It turns only when the tracing arm moves sideways, at right angles to its own length. With the pole outside the outline, the net turning of the wheel over one complete tracing, multiplied by the arm’s length, gives the area enclosed.12 Green’s theorem, a result from calculus that ties the area inside a loop to measurements taken along its edge, explains why. The same theorem is behind the shoelace formula, which a GIS uses to compute the area of a polygon, a shape stored as a list of corners.
The smaller the patch, the less accurate the planimeter was. Tests reported in a 1903 manual put its average error at about 0.08% on a figure of 200 cm² and about 2.6% on one of 5 cm².11 A good reading also depended on the person and the paper. A geographer at the State University of Iowa who was arguing for dot grids put it this way: the reading “will be accurate if the operator has a very steady hand and traces the boundary with utmost care, and if the surface of the map is neither too smooth nor too rough.”13 Forest Service guidance was to trace each patch at least twice and average the readings.14
Counting was the alternative. A transparent sheet ruled into small squares turned area into a tally, but the technician had to judge every square the boundary cut through, and the results drifted. With squares, the same Iowa geographer warned, “the same area measured on successive days by the same operator may appear to have either grown or shrunk in the meantime.”13 Forests do grow, but not overnight. A grid of dots removed most of that judgment. Each dot stood for a fixed area at the map’s scale, and the technician counted the dots inside the outline. In a Forest Service test, dots were off by 1.84% on average and squares by 4.50%, and counting dots took two-thirds as long as counting squares.15
The Forest Service printed its dot grids on transparent cards, like the one from its Pacific Northwest station in Fig. 4, with grids of 16 and 64 dots per square inch and a table of acres per dot at eight map scales.16 The more dots that fell inside a patch, the more reliable the estimate. Two cartographers later estimated that a count of about 100 dots inside a patch has a standard error, the typical size of its miss, of roughly 1.5% of the area. Their example of a job the method suited was measuring “the total area of woodland shown on a map.”17


Fig. 4Timber Survey Aid No. 6, a Forest Service card of square and dot grids with a table of acres per dot. At 1:63,360, where an inch is a mile, each dot of the 64-dot grid stands for 10 acres.Card: U.S. Forest Service, Pacific Northwest Forest and Range Experiment Station, undated · Public domain · Flickr

The finer grid on the card meant four times as many dots to count, the price of a more reliable answer. Shape mattered too. Real boundaries curve and wander, and a 1975 study in the Canadian Journal of Forest Research found that a count’s error depends on a patch’s shape as well as on how many dots fall inside it.18



                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  



Fig. 5How a dot count works: a grid of dots laid over two outlined patches. Only the dots inside the outlines are counted, and each stands for a fixed area of ground.Drawing: The Shape-Files · illustration, no real location

title: The Map Room: Answering Geographic Questions by Hand
section: Finally, add it up, and start again
text:
Finally, add it up, and start again
The last job was arithmetic: add up the patches for each owner and each reporting area, sheet by sheet. The Forest Service’s 1979 summary reports Oregon’s damage by reporting area.3
Done carefully, all of this produced a good answer, but only to the question that was asked. Ask how much of the damage fell in each watershed instead of on each owner’s land, and the damage outlines could be reused, but every patch had to be split along new lines, measured, and added up again. The registered sheets and the outlines were the only parts of the job that a new question could share.

title: The Map Room: Answering Geographic Questions by Hand
section: A country’s worth of sheets
text:
A country’s worth of sheets
One question on one pair of sheets was slow enough. The Canada Land Inventory faced the same work across a whole country. Approved by the federal government in October 1963, the Canada Land Inventory set out to map about 2.6 million km² (a million square miles). It recorded how the land was used and what it could support for agriculture, forestry, recreation, and wildlife.19,20 Its land-use mappers worked on those same 1:50,000 sheets wherever they existed. Elsewhere, they took whatever base they could find, from about 1:40,000 to 1:63,360, rescaled it photographically to 1:50,000, and traced it onto blank sheets of drafting film “prepared to a master grid.”21
The inventory planned on a computer from the outset. Roger Tomlinson, its data processing coordinator, put the start of the system’s design in 1963.20 The inventory’s program report later explained why: “Conventional methods of map compilation, area measurement and comparison between maps and statistical tables, would have imposed severe restrictions on the inventory program.”19 When Tomlinson described the inventory’s “geo-information system” in 1967, he defined the system’s central task by the hand method it was replacing. Overlay was “the well-known function of putting one map over another and examining the resultant data relationships,” and, “as with the manual method of overlaying maps,” the maps had to be “at a common scale and frame size.” The computer still needed every map traced by hand, but only once. After that, the overlays and the measuring were its job.20
Computers didn’t empty the map rooms quickly. Sixteen years after the inventory’s decision, the Forest Service crews behind Fig. 1 were still measuring by hand. The Pacific Northwest Region kept tracing and tallying by hand until 1988, when it got access to MOSS, a GIS the agency’s own history calls the Map Overlay Statistical System.1,2

title: The Map Room: Answering Geographic Questions by Hand
section: Where it shows up today
text:
Where it shows up today
In a GIS, the same four jobs remain, done by software under new names. Making the sheets agree is now the job of coordinate reference systems, which tie coordinates to places on the Earth, and of the conversions between them. In QGIS, a free desktop GIS, each map is a layer of stored shapes, and laying one over another is a single run of the Intersection tool, which “extracts the portions of features from the input layer that overlap features in the overlay layer.”22 The software computes each patch’s area from its corners, using the same mathematics as the planimeter, and adds up the totals for each owner in one more step. Because the outlines are stored, the watershed question is one more run of the same tool with a different second layer, not a new tracing and a new count.
The Forest Service’s old survey maps went into the GIS too. As each one was digitized, the region replaced the totals its staff had counted by hand with totals computed from the stored outlines.2 The maps no longer had to be traced and measured again for every new question. Their geography was stored, ready to be overlaid, measured, and counted whenever the next question came along.

title: How Humans Learned to Measure the Earth
text:
Open a map on your phone, and a blue dot finds you. The phone works out your latitude and longitude on a model of the Earth called WGS 84, the World Geodetic System 1984 used by the Global Positioning System (GPS).1 The model is a slightly squashed ball called an ellipsoid. From its center to the equator is 6,378,137 meters, and from its center to either pole is about 21 kilometers less.2 The ellipsoid is defined by two numbers, one for the Earth’s size and one for its squash. The phone needs only a few seconds to find you, but working out those two numbers took people about 2,000 years.
In File 001, The Map Room, the Earth’s curve showed up as the thin gaps that rows of flat map sheets would, in theory, leave when laid edge to edge. How curved it is, and in what shape, is a much older question. Latitude was the easier part. North of the equator, the height of the celestial pole, the point in the sky that the stars turn around, tells you roughly how far north you are. The hard part was turning degrees in the sky into distance on the ground. People could measure one degree of latitude, which is the distance you travel north before the stars shift by one degree. Comparing degrees measured far apart is how they learned the Earth’s shape.

title: How Humans Learned to Measure the Earth
section: Eratosthenes needed a shadow and a distance
text:
Eratosthenes needed a shadow and a distance
In the third century BC, the Greek scholar Eratosthenes started from two Egyptian cities he took to lie on the same north–south line. At noon on the summer solstice, sundials at Syene, far up the Nile, cast no shadow, because the sun stood straight overhead. At Alexandria the shadow in a bowl-shaped sundial covered 1/50 of a full circle. He used a distance of 5,000 stadia between the cities (a stadion was an ancient Greek unit of distance) and concluded that the whole Earth was 50 times that distance, or 250,000 stadia around.3,4
Sunlight arrives in parallel rays, so the slant of the shadow at Alexandria equals the angle between the two cities at the Earth’s center (Fig. 1). If that angle is 1/50 of a circle, the distance between the cities is 1/50 of the way around. This method of finding the Earth’s size is called arc measurement. Every survey in this story uses it.




The top of a curved Earth under vertical rays of sunlight. An upright pin at Syene lines up with a ray; a pin at Alexandria leans away from the rays. One arc marks the angle between a ray and the leaning pin, and a matching arc marks the angle between the two cities’ radii, with 5,000 stadia labeled along the surface between them


      Sunlight at noon,in parallel rays       Syene: no shadow Alexandria Shadow angle: 1/50 of a circle Shadow angle at Alexandria: 1/50 of a circle 5,000 stadia 5,000 stadia  Same angle at the center



Fig. 1Eratosthenes’ method, as the only detailed ancient account describes it. Parallel sunlight casts no shadow at Syene and a slanting one at Alexandria, and the slant equals the angle between the two cities at the Earth’s center. The angle is drawn far larger than the account’s 1/50 of a circle (7.2°) so it can be seen.Drawing: The Shape-Files · illustration, not to scale


The famous well at Syene, lit to the bottom by the noon sun, comes from other ancient writers and isn’t part of his method.5,6 The only detailed account of the method, written two centuries or more later by the Greek writer Cleomedes, treats the 5,000 stadia as an assumption, and nobody knows how long Eratosthenes’ stadion was. Depending on which length you assume, his Earth comes out slightly too small or about 16% too large.7 The weak link was the distance.

title: How Humans Learned to Measure the Earth
section: Triangles made the distance measurable
text:
Triangles made the distance measurable
The distance remained the weak link for centuries. In the 1520s Jean Fernel tried a different approach. He went north from Paris until the celestial pole stood a degree higher, then rode home in a coach, counted the turns of its wheel, and subtracted a guess for the road’s bends and hills. His answer came so close that a later surveyor concluded Fernel’s guess for the road must have offset an error elsewhere in his work.8
In 1615 the Dutch mathematician Willebrord Snellius found a way around the problem. He measured a short base on the ground, about 328 meters, and took everything else as angles between church towers. Once one side and the angles of a triangle are known, its other sides can be calculated, and one of those sides becomes the starting side of the next triangle. Through a chain of such triangles, Snellius stretched his 328 meters into the 130 kilometers between Alkmaar and Bergen op Zoom. This was the first arc measurement made by triangulation.9
His triangles were sound, but his latitude measurements, read from the sky with open sights instead of telescopes, were not, and his degree came out 3.5% short.10 One of his towers was hardly needed: Gouda’s tower already anchored that part of the network. Snellius added nearby Oudewater anyway, and the geodesist who recomputed the survey concludes that he wanted to visit his widowed mother there.9
Half a century later, Jean Picard, an astronomer of the Académie des sciences in Paris, fixed the weak point by putting telescopes with crosshairs on his instruments, both for the angles between stations and for the stars. South of Paris, he measured an 11-kilometer base along a straight paved road, using rods made from wooden pike shafts. From there he extended the measurement north toward Amiens through 13 triangles (Fig. 2).8


Fig. 2The southern end of Picard’s chain of triangles, from a 1740 reprint of his survey. The base runs from A (Villejuif) to B (Juvisy), and the chain continues north beyond this detail to Amiens.Map: Dheulland after Jean Picard, 1740 · Public domain · Internet Archive · cropped to a detail

Picard’s degree came to 57,060 toises. A toise was a French measure of about 1.95 meters, so his degree was about 111.2 kilometers, which is very close to the true length there. Later checks found errors in his work that, as a 19th-century historian put it, “by accident almost balanced each other,” so the closeness was partly luck.11

title: How Humans Learned to Measure the Earth
section: A short pendulum raised a harder question
text:
A short pendulum raised a harder question
One degree, however well measured, can’t reveal a shape. On a perfect sphere every degree is the same length, so the test is to compare degrees measured far apart. The first hint that the Earth isn’t a sphere came from a pendulum. A pendulum’s swing depends on gravity. If it is adjusted to beat seconds, its length gives a way to compare the strength of gravity in different places. In 1672 the astronomer Jean Richer, sent to Cayenne in South America, found that his seconds pendulum had to be made shorter there than in Paris to keep time.12 Near the equator, gravity pulled a little less.
Isaac Newton explained why in his Principia of 1687. The Earth’s rotation slightly reduces the apparent pull of gravity at the equator. It also makes the Earth bulge there, putting a pendulum farther from the center. Newton estimated that the poles sit about 1/230 of the Earth’s radius closer to the center than the equator does. That ratio, the difference between the two radii as a fraction of the larger, is called the flattening.13,14
Newton’s bulge could be tested on the ground. Walk north and the ground curves under you, so straight down, the line a plumb bob hangs along, tilts against the stars. One degree of latitude is how far you walk for it to tilt by one degree. Where the Earth is flatter, the ground curves more gently, so you walk farther for the same tilt. On a flattened Earth, degrees get longer toward the poles.15
The Paris Observatory’s own survey said the opposite. By 1718 Jacques Cassini and his father had run a chain of triangles through Paris from Dunkirk to Collioure, near the Spanish border. Their arc was six times longer than Picard’s, and it showed degrees shrinking northward.16 By the rule above, degrees that shrink toward the pole mean an Earth stretched toward the poles, like an egg standing on end. Now there were two answers. Newton had a theory and a pendulum, and the Cassinis had a survey across the whole of France.
Neither side could be sure. From one degree to the next, the Cassinis’ degrees changed by only about 60 meters. An error of just 2 arcseconds in a star sighting could produce a change that large, and 2 arcseconds is about the width of a quarter seen from 2.5 kilometers.17

title: How Humans Learned to Measure the Earth
section: Lapland and Peru showed which way the Earth is squashed
text:
Lapland and Peru showed which way the Earth is squashed
The instruments of 1718 couldn’t settle a change that small. The Académie’s answer was two arc measurements as far apart as it could reach. If Newton was right, a degree near the Arctic Circle would be longer than one at the equator, and if the Cassinis were right, it would be shorter. In 1735 one party sailed for the equator, near Quito, in what is now Ecuador, which the French then counted as part of Peru.18,19 In 1736 another went to Lapland, at the Arctic Circle, then part of Sweden.
The Arctic party, led by Pierre-Louis Moreau de Maupertuis, set its triangles on hilltops along the Torne River valley and measured its base on the river itself once it froze, starting on the winter solstice. Two teams measured the same 14 kilometers of ice and differed by about 11 centimeters. It was cold enough that even brandy, the only drink they could keep liquid, left their lips and tongues stuck to the cup.15,20
The result went Newton’s way: Lapland’s degree came out longer than any degree measured in France. The Cassinis’ supporters in Paris resisted it.21 Maupertuis was portrayed in Lapland furs with one hand pressing down on a globe (Fig. 3), and Voltaire, then his friend, took to calling him a flattener. In one letter Voltaire addressed him as “my dear flattener of worlds and of Cassinis.”22


Fig. 3Maupertuis in Lapland furs, his hand on a globe, in a 1741 engraving after a portrait by Robert Levrac-Tournières. The verse on the ledge is by Voltaire.Engraving: Jean Daullé and Johann Georg Wille, 1741 · Public domain · Wellcome Collection

The Peru party took far longer. It measured a base on the high plain of Yaruquí (Fig. 4) and carried a chain of more than 30 triangles south through the Andes.23 At one festival, young clowns who had watched the astronomers at work mimicked them in the arena with quadrants of wood and painted paper, and Charles-Marie de La Condamine, one of the party’s three French academicians, “saw nothing more amusing during the ten years of the voyage.” In August 1739 the party’s surgeon was attacked by a mob at a bullfight in Cuenca.18 La Condamine wrote that the surgeon “died four days later of his wounds, in my bed.”19


Fig. 4The plain of Yaruquí, near Quito, where the Peru party measured its base, with the Andes behind it, from La Condamine’s account of 1751. The numbers along the horizon belong to a key below the view, not shown here.Engraving: from La Condamine’s Journal du voyage, 1751, Universidad de Sevilla · Public domain · Internet Archive · cropped to the view

Corrected to sea level, Peru’s degree came within about 34 meters of today’s value, and it was more than a kilometer shorter than Lapland’s.23 France, meanwhile, had reversed itself. Jacques Cassini’s son, César-François Cassini de Thury, remeasured the French meridian from 1739, and in 1744 he concluded that the degrees shrink toward the equator, “and consequently that the figure of the Earth is flattened.”17 Newton had won the argument over the direction. The amount was another matter. Depending on which degrees they compared, estimates of the Earth’s flattening ranged from more than twice the true value to nearly the right answer (Fig. 5).17,23




Length of one degree of latitude by latitude: the WGS 84 curve rises from 110.57 km at the equator to 111.69 km at the poles. Their report blamed the instrument used for those sightings, which the slightest bend on the long trip north could have thrown off, and it ruled out the pull of the nearby mountains on the plumb line.24 Lapland’s error was bigger than the real difference between a Lapland degree and a French one, so Lapland alone had proved little. The verdict held because Peru and the new French survey carried it.

title: How Humans Learned to Measure the Earth
section: It took satellites to measure how much
text:
It took satellites to measure how much
That verdict settled which way the Earth is squashed, but not by how much. An ellipsoid, the shape you get by spinning an ellipse about its short axis, needs only two numbers: the radius at the equator and the flattening. From the 1830s on, geodesists fitted ellipsoids to the arcs they had, and different countries adopted different ones. North America used the Clarke ellipsoid of 1866.25,26 The equatorial radii of these ellipsoids differ by more than a kilometer, because each was fitted to different arcs on a planet that isn’t smooth.
Gravity defines another surface, called the geoid. It is an irregular level surface that follows mean sea level and continues beneath the continents. Because gravity acts at right angles to it, a plumb line hangs perpendicular to the geoid, not necessarily to a smooth ellipsoid.25 The geoid falls about 106 meters below the ellipsoid south of India and rises as much as 85 meters above it elsewhere (Fig. 6).27 Where the geoid slopes, the direction of a plumb line shifts too, so a latitude measured from the stars can differ slightly from the latitude on the ellipsoid.


Fig. 6The geoid from satellite gravity data, with its heights exaggerated 10,000 times. Blue lies below a smooth ellipsoid and red above it.Diagram: Mark SubbaRao, NASA Scientific Visualization Studio, from the GOCO06s gravity model, 2026 · Public domain · NASA SVS

Satellites finally measured the flattening. The Earth’s equatorial bulge pulls unevenly on a satellite and slowly turns the plane of its orbit, at a rate that depends on the size of the bulge. By 1959 the orbits of Sputnik 2 and Vanguard 1 put the flattening at about 1/298.28,29 Later satellites refined that into WGS 84, which keeps the equatorial radius at 6,378,137 meters and sets the flattening at 1/298.257223563.2

title: How Humans Learned to Measure the Earth
section: Every coordinate still rests on those two numbers
text:
Every coordinate still rests on those two numbers
Every geographic coordinate system names an ellipsoid. A shapefile keeps its coordinate system in a small file beside it, the .prj, and for WGS 84 the two numbers are written out in plain text: 6378137, and 298.257223563, the inverse of the flattening.30,31 Much of North America’s older mapping used the Clarke ellipsoid, about 69 meters larger at the equator.26 Moving such data onto WGS 84 takes more than swapping one ellipsoid for another, but it starts with the file saying which Earth it was drawn on. Which Earth, and where it sits on the real one, is the subject of File 003, Latitude, Longitude and the Datum Problem.
Back on the phone, the blue dot rests on those two numbers. By those numbers, someone standing at 40° north, roughly the latitude of Philadelphia, is about 4,430 kilometers from the equator. On a sphere built from Snellius’ short degree, that distance would be about 135 kilometers shorter. On a perfect sphere built from Picard’s degree, it would be about 19 kilometers too long, because a sphere leaves out the squash. The phone computes the degree under your feet from a model built one measured degree at a time.

title: About The Shape-Files
text:
The Shape-Files tells the story of how geography became something computers can store, search and reason about. It starts in the map rooms where people answered questions with tracing paper and a ruler, and follows the thread through the first computer systems of the 1960s, the databases and workstations that came after, desktop GIS and open-source software, all the way to cloud-native data and the AI agents that work with maps today.

A new file comes out every week. Each one takes a single idea, format, algorithm or system and shows where it came from and how it works. The history is told with diagrams and worked examples, and the files on today’s tools add code you can run yourself. Read them in order as one long history, or jump to any topic that piques your interest.
It’s written for anyone who works with maps or spatial data and wants to know why the tools behave the way they do: GIS analysts, developers, data engineers, students, and anyone who has ever wondered why a shapefile comes in pieces.
The Shape-Files is written by Jacob Hogue.

title: Map Projections: Flattening a Curved Earth
text:
On August 2, 2018, Google Maps told its followers that on its desktop map, “Greenland’s projection is no longer the size of Africa. Just zoom all the way out.”1 Zoomed all the way out, the map had become a globe. Zoom in to a street, though, and web maps are flat again. They draw every street on one flat map, a descendant of a chart made for sailors in 1569.2,3
In File 003, Latitude, Longitude and the Datum Problem, coordinates were angles, measured on a curved model of the Earth that a datum pins to the real one. But screens and paper are flat, and so are the grids most measurements are worked out on. A map projection is the rule that turns latitude and longitude into flat x and y.4 The flattening always costs something. Measured in a web map’s own units, a field near Meades Ranch, the Kansas survey station from File 003, comes out with about two-thirds more area than it has. Every flat map keeps some things true and lets others go, and which ones it keeps depends on what the map is for.
The station’s datasheet, from the National Geodetic Survey, shows that choice made twice. Its mark, a disk set in concrete when the station was reset, has two flat addresses, one on a Kansas state grid and one on a worldwide grid called the Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM), both in meters.5 The datasheet also says how much each grid shrinks or stretches distances at the mark. Why does one mark need two flat addresses, and why can’t either one keep distances true?

title: Map Projections: Flattening a Curved Earth
section: Mercator kept the directions
text:
Mercator kept the directions
Sailors in the sixteenth century needed a flat chart that kept one thing true. A navigator steered one compass bearing at a time and plotted it with a ruler, so a straight line on the chart had to be a line of constant bearing. The usual charts spaced the parallels evenly and drew every degree of longitude as wide as it is at the equator. At the latitude of Kansas, such a chart drew the land about 1.29 times too wide but kept its north–south size. That threw off the angles between courses, so a line of constant bearing came out curved.6,7 Gerard Mercator, a mapmaker in Duisburg, fixed this with his world map of 1569 (Fig. 1). One of its legends explains that he “gradually increased the degrees of latitude toward each pole in proportion to the lengthening of the parallels.”6


Fig. 1Mercator’s world map of 1569, engraved on copper. This copy is printed on 18 sheets. The parallels spread farther apart toward the top and bottom. The map stops short of the North Pole because, as one of its legends says, the degrees of latitude would “run out to infinity,” so the far north is redrawn on the round inset at lower left.Map: Gerard Mercator, Duisburg, 1569, Universitätsbibliothek Basel, UBH Kartenslg AA 3-5 · Public domain · e-rara

His rule was to stretch every place north–south by the same amount it was already stretched east–west. At the latitude of Kansas both stretches are 1.29, so small shapes and the angles between courses come out true, and a straight line on the chart is a constant bearing. Areas, though, are stretched both ways, so at that latitude they come out about two-thirds too big. Only the equator is drawn at true size, and the stretch grows toward the poles.7 The same rule draws Greenland about 16 times its real size. On the map it looks about as big as Africa, which is really about 14 times larger.8
Mercator never explained how he spaced his parallels. Edward Wright, an English mathematician, published the arithmetic in 1599 and said where it came from: “the way how this should be done, I learned neither of Mercator, nor any man els.”9 He added up the stretch minute by minute of latitude, and his table of the spacing ends at 90° with the single word “Infinite.” To explain the result, he asked readers to picture a globe “inscribed into a concaue cylinder” that would “swel like a bladder,” stretching “as much in longitude as in latitude,” until it pressed flat against the cylinder (Fig. 2). It is a picture of even stretching. A common story has the chart made by shining a light through a globe onto a cylinder, but no such construction gives Mercator’s spacing.7


Fig. 2Wright’s grid for a Mercator chart, from his book of 1599. The equator runs along the bottom, the parallels spread apart as they climb toward the pole, and the slanting lines of constant compass bearing stay straight.Map: Edward Wright, Certaine Errors in Nauigation, London, 1599 · CC BY 4.0 · Courtesy of the John Carter Brown Library · cropped to the plate

title: Map Projections: Flattening a Curved Earth
section: No flat map can keep everything
text:
No flat map can keep everything
Mercator kept directions and gave up size. In 1772 the mathematician Johann Heinrich Lambert explained why every map has to give up something. He listed what a perfect map would do: keep the shapes of countries and their relative sizes, keep distances in proportion, draw the shortest routes as straight lines, and make latitude and longitude easy to read. All of it would be easy, he wrote, “if the Earth’s surface were a plane. But it is a spherical surface, and so not all conditions can be satisfied at once.”10 A triangle on the globe shows the problem. Two meridians that leave the North Pole 90° apart both meet the equator at right angles, so the three lines enclose a triangle with three right angles. No flat triangle can have that. In 1827 the German mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss proved the general rule. A surface can be bent without stretching or tearing, but bending never changes its curvature, and since a flat sheet has none, nobody can lay a globe flat without stretching it.11

title: Map Projections: Flattening a Curved Earth
section: Tissot gave distortion a shape
text:
Tissot gave distortion a shape
Since every flat map stretches, mapmakers needed a way to measure how much, and where. Auguste Tissot gave them one in 1859, in a note to the French Academy of Sciences. Close up, he found, any map stretches the ground like a rubber sheet pulled in two directions at right angles, sometimes harder one way than the other.12 A tiny circle on the ground therefore becomes an ellipse on the map, and its size and shape show how the map stretches at that spot. The stretch in a given direction is called the scale factor. It compares a short length on the map with the map’s stated scale, so 1 means true and 1.29 means 29 percent too long.7 Fig. 3 puts the same circles, each 1,000 kilometers across on the ground, on two world maps.




Two world maps, one above the other, each scattered with gray circles of the same size on the ground, with two magenta circles, one in Kansas and one on Greenland. On the upper map the circles grow toward the top and bottom; on the lower map they keep their size and flatten toward the edges.


Mercator (conformal): angles kept, areas grow                                                                                Meades Ranch  Greenland Equal Earth (equal-area): areas kept, shapes squashed                                                                                Meades Ranch  Greenland



Fig. 3The same circles, each 1,000 kilometers across on the ground, on a Mercator map (top) and on Equal Earth, an equal-area map (bottom). Mercator keeps the circles nearly round and lets them grow toward the poles. Equal Earth keeps their areas and squashes their shapes. The magenta circles are centered on Meades Ranch and on Greenland.Drawing: The Shape-Files · coastlines from Natural Earth · illustration


On the Mercator map the circles stay round, or nearly. At any one point Mercator’s map stretches equally in every direction, so a small enough circle would stay perfectly round, and one scale factor describes the stretch there. That property is called conformal, and it keeps angles and the shapes of small features. The circles in Fig. 3 are large enough that the stretch changes across each one, so the circle on Greenland bulges toward the pole. It is also drawn more than three times as wide as a circle on the equator. On the equal-area map every circle covers the same area of paper, but away from the center the circles are squashed into ellipses. A map can have either property, but as the US Geological Survey’s manual of projections puts it, “No map can be both equal-area and conformal.”7

title: Map Projections: Flattening a Curved Earth
section: Small zones keep the stretch small
text:
Small zones keep the stretch small
Many projections have lines they keep true, like Mercator’s equator, and the stretch generally grows with distance from them.7 A map of a small area can do better than one true line down its middle. Draw the whole map slightly small, and the one true line becomes two, one on each side of the middle. Between them distances come out a little short, and beyond them a little long, so the error is shared out instead of piling up toward the edges. Across a narrow zone it stays tiny. Lambert’s conformal conic, one of the projections he introduced, can be set so that two parallels of latitude are true. It can be pictured as a cone that passes through the globe along those two parallels and is then unrolled flat.13,14 It suits a state that is long from east to west and narrow from north to south, which is the shape of Kansas.
The state grids began with that kind of map. Early in 1933 George F. Syme, of North Carolina’s highway commission, asked the US Coast and Geodetic Survey for a system of plane coordinates for his state.15 Surveyors work with angles and distances, and on a flat grid they could use “only the formulas of plane surveying.”14 Oscar S. Adams, a mathematician at the Survey, designed the system on Lambert’s conic, and he wanted it on record that the idea came from engineers, “not as a result of a brain storm of some theoretical mathematician and geodesist.”15 Zones were kept narrow enough to hold errors to 1 part in 10,000, or 10 centimeters in a kilometer, with a few exceptions. Within about a year every state had a grid designed for it, and Kansas got two zones, Kansas North and Kansas South. Together the grids are now called the State Plane Coordinate System.14,16
A grid for one state was no use to an army working across continents. According to the US Geological Survey, the US Army adopted the UTM grid in 1947 for military maps of the whole world.7 UTM uses the transverse Mercator, which is Mercator’s map turned on its side, so that the line it keeps true runs north–south instead of along the equator. Lambert had invented it for the sphere, and later mathematicians fitted it to the ellipsoid. Outside the polar regions the world is cut into 60 north–south strips, or zones, and the middle of each zone is drawn 0.9996 of true size, 40 centimeters short in every kilometer. That puts two true lines about 180 kilometers either side of the middle.7 UTM’s zones are much wider than a state’s, so near the equator their edges come out as much as 1 part in 1,000 too long, a meter in every kilometer. When the state grids were redone in the 1980s for the new North American Datum of 1983 (NAD 83), the states kept their own grids rather than switch. Most American surveyors and engineers still considered UTM “unacceptable because of rapidly changing grid scale factors.”16
The Meades Ranch datasheet shows both designs at work. The Kansas North grid draws distances at the mark 4.3 centimeters short in every kilometer, measured against the ellipsoid, File 002’s Earth model. UTM zone 14 draws them 38 centimeters short.5 Both are short because the mark sits between each grid’s two true lines, and UTM’s error is about nine times larger because its zone is so much wider (Fig. 4). The pasture’s height matters as well, more than the Kansas grid does. It sits 574 meters above the ellipsoid, and bringing a kilometer measured there down to the ellipsoid shortens it by 9 centimeters, twice what the grid takes off. The datasheet prints a factor for that too, so a surveyor can turn grid distances back into distances on the ground.5

title: Map Projections: Flattening a Curved Earth
section: A flat address names its datum and its projection
text:
A flat address names its datum and its projection
The Kansas address has three parts: File 003’s NAD 83, unchanged; Adams’s conic, with a handful of fixed numbers; and axes in meters. The international standard for coordinates calls that combination a projected coordinate reference system.17 Because the datum stays the same and the projection’s numbers are fixed by definition rather than measured, the standard counts the projection as a coordinate conversion, which “introduces no error into the output coordinates.” The arithmetic is exact. Distances on the map are still stretched, but the stretch is part of the definition, which is why the datasheet can print it to eight decimal places. A change of datum is a coordinate transformation instead. Its parameter values “are empirically derived,” fitted to measurements, and they carry those measurements’ errors.17 So when two layers disagree, the projection’s arithmetic is rarely to blame. More often someone has tagged one of them with the wrong datum, zone, or units.
Web maps made a different choice. To make aerial images from many sources line up, they use one projection for the whole world. They chose Mercator because, as Microsoft’s mapping documentation puts it, “Square buildings should appear square, not rectangular.”3 And because the map is “used only for map display,” the documentation goes on, a simpler version will do. That version, now called Web Mercator, applies formulas meant for a sphere to latitudes and longitudes measured on the ellipsoid, so it looks like Mercator’s map but isn’t quite conformal.18 In 2007 the developers of OpenLayers, an open-source library for web maps, gave it a code of their own, 900913, which spells “Google” in digits. The first reply to the announcement pointed out that the proper hacker spelling would be 600613.19 Later that year the registry that catalogs coordinate systems declined to list Web Mercator. It relented in 2008, but its entry still calls Web Mercator “Not a recognised geodetic system.”18
In a web map’s own units, the Meades Ranch mark sits about 4,754 kilometers north of the equator. Along the ground it is about 4,343. At that latitude every kilometer on the ground measures about 1.29 kilometers in map units, the same stretch Mercator’s chart gave Kansas. Draw a 1-kilometer buffer around the mark in those units, and it covers only about 775 meters. The fix is to measure distances on a local grid such as the state’s, and areas on an equal-area map. Esri’s documentation puts it more bluntly: lengths and areas in Web Mercator “are not accurate or valid.”20

title: Map Projections: Flattening a Curved Earth
section: One mark, three flat addresses
text:
One mark, three flat addresses
None of that shows on the screen. Zoom in on the pasture at Meades Ranch, and the web map is flat again, with anything square on the ground looking square, or close to it. That is what it was built for. So the mark has three flat addresses. The Kansas grid’s is for surveyors in Kansas, UTM’s is for anyone who needs one grid around the world, and the web map’s is for anyone who just wants to look.

title: Latitude, Longitude and the Datum Problem
text:
Visitors to the Royal Observatory in Greenwich, London, can stand on the Prime Meridian, a line set into the courtyard that marks zero degrees of longitude. If they check the coordinates on their phones, they find they are not at zero. A 2015 paper by five scientists in the Journal of Geodesy worked out that they would have to walk about 102 meters east before their phones read zero longitude.1 The obvious guess is that Britain has drifted since Greenwich was chosen in 1884. It has, but only by a few meters, and nobody has moved the line.1
Small as it is, that gap points to a problem anyone who combines maps eventually meets. File 002, How Humans Learned to Measure the Earth, told how people learned the size and shape of the Earth model used to measure latitude and longitude. The numbers also depend on where that model is pinned to the real Earth, and on where longitude starts. A pair of coordinates names a place only within a particular datum. The datum defines how the mathematical model of the Earth is positioned and oriented relative to the real one. Until satellites, most countries set up their own, each from a starting point it chose. Expressed in two different datums, the same pair of numbers can land anywhere from across the street to several blocks apart, which is one reason two map layers of the same street sometimes refuse to line up.

title: Latitude, Longitude and the Datum Problem
section: Longitude was a question of time
text:
Longitude was a question of time
Latitude has a natural zero, the equator, and the stars give it to anyone who can measure an angle. Longitude has no natural zero, and it has to be measured with a clock. The Earth rotates 15° in an hour, so the difference between local time and the time at some other place is a difference in longitude. If the sun is at its highest where you are, which makes it local noon, and a clock still set to the time at home says 3 p.m., you are 3 hours behind home, or 45° west of it.
On land, astronomers could compare times by watching the same event in the sky, such as the eclipse of one of Jupiter’s moons. At sea, a ship needed a clock that kept home time for weeks, and no clock could. In 1714 Isaac Newton told a committee of the House of Commons that such a watch “hath not yet been made,” because of “the Motion of a Ship, the Variation of Heat and Cold, Wet and Dry, and the Difference of Gravity in different Latitudes.”2 Parliament’s Longitude Act that year offered £20,000 for a method that found longitude to within half a degree.3
The clockmaker John Harrison built such a watch. After a trial voyage to Barbados in 1764, the Board of Longitude, the commissioners who judged the prize, agreed that his watch, H4, had kept time within the Act’s strictest limit. It would not certify him as the winner until he showed how the watch was made.4 A good clock told a navigator his longitude relative to the place whose time it kept. It did not say which place that should be.
The rival method used the moon as a clock. The moon moves against the stars fast enough that the angle between it and a bright star, measured from the deck, tells the time at any place for which those angles have been worked out in advance. Nevil Maskelyne, the Astronomer Royal, made the method practical with the first Nautical Almanac, for the year 1767 (Fig. 1). Most of its tables, the lunar distances among them, were “computed by Two separate Persons, and examined by a Third,” and “all the Calculations are made according to apparent Time by the Meridian of the Royal Observatory at Greenwich.”5 A navigator who used the tables found Greenwich time, and so counted longitude from Greenwich.


Fig. 1A page of the first Nautical Almanac, for January 1767. Each row gives the angle between the moon’s center and a bright star or the sun at noon and every 3 hours after, Greenwich time. A navigator who measured the same angle at sea could read off the time at Greenwich.Scan: Commissioners of Longitude, The Nautical Almanac and Astronomical Ephemeris, for the Year 1767, 1766 · Public domain · Internet Archive · cropped to the table

title: Latitude, Longitude and the Datum Problem
section: Greenwich became zero by a vote
text:
Greenwich became zero by a vote
Other countries kept their own zeros. By the 1880s, maps and charts counted longitude from Paris, Cádiz, Lisbon, and several other observatories, so a longitude meant little until you knew which zero it was counted from.6
In October 1884 delegates from more than 20 nations met in Washington, D.C. A table of the world’s shipping presented there showed that ships using charts counted from Greenwich carried 72% of the world’s tonnage. The delegates voted to propose a single zero of longitude to their governments, the meridian through Airy’s transit circle at the Royal Observatory (Fig. 2). Only San Domingo (the Dominican Republic) voted against, and France and Brazil abstained.6


Fig. 2The Royal Observatory on Greenwich Hill in 1824, in a print lettered “Flamstead House,” its spelling of Flamsteed House. Airy’s transit circle, the instrument the 1884 vote named, was installed at the observatory 27 years later.Engraving: aquatint after Thomas Hosmer Shepherd, 1824 · Public domain · Wellcome Collection

A meridian is a flat plane that slices the Earth from pole to pole, and the zero meridian is the one that runs through that instrument. George Airy had installed the transit circle at the observatory a generation earlier. It is a telescope that turns only in the north–south plane, so its observers could time each star as it crossed the meridian.1 The conference recommended a zero for longitude. Contrary to a common story, it did not create time zones.6
France kept its own zero at Paris. Paris lies east of Greenwich, so its clocks ran about 9 minutes ahead. In 1911 France adopted Greenwich time, in a law that never mentions Greenwich. It set the legal time of France as “Paris mean time, set back by nine minutes twenty-one seconds.”7

title: Latitude, Longitude and the Datum Problem
section: A continent was pinned to a pasture in Kansas
text:
A continent was pinned to a pasture in Kansas
A shared zero told every country where to start counting longitude. It did not say where each country’s Earth model sat on the ground. In the United States the answer was a pasture ridge at Meades Ranch, in Osborne County, Kansas (Fig. 3). Surveyors of the US Coast and Geodetic Survey had marked a triangulation station there in 1891. Under a marble post they buried the station’s underground mark, the part meant to survive if anyone disturbed the post. Like the marks at many of the Survey’s stations in Kansas, it was “a bottle filled with ashes.”8 In 1901 the Survey defined its national datum by this station’s coordinates, and the North American Datum of 1927 kept them.8,9


Fig. 3A Coast and Geodetic Survey truck at the Meades Ranch station, about 1934 by NOAA’s dating. The square slab in the grass is probably the station’s marker.Photo: NOAA National Geodetic Survey · Public domain · NOAA Digital Library

For the old datums, a starting point and a direction fixed the model in place. Surveyors chose an ellipsoid, the Earth model from File 002, and gave the starting point its latitude and longitude. They also fixed the direction from the starting point to a neighboring station, which set how the model was turned. Every other station in the network took its coordinates from triangles measured outward from the start. The model the US used was the Clarke ellipsoid, which File 002 named near its end.8,9
Starting coordinates came from the stars, measured with instruments leveled by gravity. A plumb line hangs along the local pull of gravity, and mountains and uneven rock tilt that pull very slightly, as File 002 described, so any single sighting carries a small tilt of its own. The Survey did not rely on one spot. Its coordinates for Meades Ranch had not been measured from the stars in Kansas. Instead, they were carried there through the chain of triangles from a station in Maryland, whose position combined more than a hundred astronomical observations.9,10 A check against hundreds of stations across the country then showed that the datum came close to the best fit for the United States.8
A good fit to one country was also the limit. Geodesy for the Layman, a handbook of the Defense Mapping Agency, says of the continental datums that each ellipsoid “is an adequate fit in the area of the origin,” but that neither “provides a good fit for the entire earth.”11 Most countries fitted their own models to their own territory in the same way. Nobody could see the Earth’s center, so nobody knew how far each national model missed it.
The 1927 network was computed by people with tables and desk calculators.10,12 As new surveys were added over the following decades, they were forced to fit coordinates that could not easily be changed. In the words of the National Geodetic Survey’s report on the next datum, the network could “produce unexpectedly large errors in unexpected places.”9

title: Latitude, Longitude and the Datum Problem
section: Satellites found the Earth’s center
text:
Satellites found the Earth’s center
Satellites measured what the old surveyors could not. By tracking satellites and modeling their orbits, geodesists could work out positions relative to the Earth’s center of mass.11 That let them pin a datum to the center of the Earth instead of to a pasture. The new North American Datum of 1983 (NAD 83) was finished in 1986. Its network was solved by computer in a single calculation and tied to positions measured from satellites.9 It has no starting point on the ground. It is still a datum, but its model is centered on what was then the best estimate of the Earth’s center of mass.12
Recomputing old coordinates on the new datum shows how far the old choices were off (Fig. 4). Meades Ranch’s coordinates moved about 30 meters west, although the mark itself stayed where it was.13 Across the lower 48 states, coordinates on the 1927 datum changed by tens of meters, and by up to about 100.9 Hawaii was never on that datum, and coordinates on its own old datum changed by about 450 meters.14

title: Latitude, Longitude and the Datum Problem
section: A file has to say which datum it uses
text:
A file has to say which datum it uses
A map file that will be combined with others needs to say which datum its numbers are on. Its coordinate reference system does that job. The file’s definition of it names the datum, along with the ellipsoid and the prime meridian, the zero of longitude. When the description is missing, the software has to be told or has to guess, and the QGIS manual warns that a wrong choice “will place your layer in the wrong position on the Earth’s surface.”15 When both datums are known but the software has no way to move coordinates between them, PROJ, the open-source library that many mapping programs use, can fall back on a shortcut its documentation calls “ballpark.” The shortcut still allows for a different zero of longitude, “Greenwich vs Paris/Rome/other historic prime meridians,” so France’s old zero is still in the software. But it “does not attempt any datum shift,” and the documentation warns that it “could lead in some cases to errors of a few hundreds of metres.”16
Even the modern datums don’t quite agree. NAD 83 and the World Geodetic System 1984 (WGS 84), which the Global Positioning System (GPS) uses, were both designed as Earth-centered systems. Their early versions were close enough that software could often treat them as equivalent, and much software still does.17,18 They are not identical, though, and in the lower 48 their coordinates now differ by a meter or two. NAD 83’s center turned out to be about 2 meters from the Earth’s, and NAD 83 is tied to the North American plate, which moves while the satellites’ frame does not.19,20
Australia faced the same drift and corrected for it in public. In 2017 Geoscience Australia announced that “Australia’s coordinates have officially moved 1.8 metres northeast,” because the continent travels about 7 centimeters a year and the national datum it had used since 1994 had fallen behind (Fig. 5). The land had been moving all along, and the new coordinates even ran ahead of it, to where the continent would be in 2020.21


Fig. 5Geoscience Australia’s graphic for the 2017 change. The grid stands for the country’s coordinates, and the arrow shows the drift they had to follow.Diagram: © Commonwealth of Australia (Geoscience Australia), 2017 · CC BY 4.0 · Geoscience Australia

The size of a mismatch is a rough guide to its cause. A gap of a meter or two suggests NAD 83 data read as WGS 84. Tens of meters suggest data on an old continental datum, such as the 1927 one. Hundreds of meters suggest an old island datum, or a shortcut that applied no datum shift at all. A point thousands of kilometers away usually means latitude and longitude were swapped, because some standards list latitude first and others longitude first.22,23 Swap the two numbers for the Greenwich line, and the point lands in the Indian Ocean, far off the coast of Somalia. These are clues, not rules. The actual shift depends on which versions of the datums are involved, where the data lies, and which transformation was used. All of these coordinates are still angles on a curved Earth, and how they become flat x and y on a map is the subject of File 004, Map Projections: Flattening a Curved Earth.

title: Latitude, Longitude and the Datum Problem
section: The courtyard line and the phone are both right
text:
The courtyard line and the phone are both right
That leaves the visitors at Greenwich. Drift is far too small to explain their 102 meters. The gap comes from how each zero was set.1 The line in the courtyard marks where the plane through Airy’s transit circle meets the ground. Its observers set the vertical with a basin of mercury, whose surface settles perpendicular to the local pull of gravity, so Airy’s plane followed the local plumb line. At Greenwich the plumb line tilts very slightly away from the direction a smooth, Earth-centered model would give, so the plane set by Airy’s telescope did not pass through the Earth’s center. When space-age measurements made an Earth-centered reference possible, the new zero meridian had to pass through the Earth’s center. It was also kept parallel to Airy’s plane, because parallel planes sweep past each star at the same moment, and that kept the time measured from the stars from jumping. Sliding the plane across to the center moved the line where it meets the ground about 102 meters east.1
So the line in the courtyard still marks zero as Airy’s telescope found it, by the plumb line on one hill above the Thames. A short walk east is the zero the phones use, set for a model centered on the whole Earth. Both are zero.
